Lead-time summary: futures drift about 30 minutes before some US macro releases; event-market leaks in the cited cases show up from hours to about half a day ahead; public shocks (a debate, an assassination attempt) show no rise before the event. The adopted cover counts the classes with 2 or more adopted sources with no risk. Only 3 sources are adopted, so the gap count shows the plans and the adopted cover shows the outcome.

The adopted cover of 24 is a measure of the distribution layer. Its two sources, nws-alerts-api and iem-vtec, fail apart (api.weather.gov and the feeds of IEM), but both carry the products of one origin, the NWS. No class of the 24 has two independent origins. The layers of the cover measure this at this time: 24 classes have 2 paths, and no class has 2 origins.
Round 1 searched 39 queries and 58 lists. Round 2 starts with the sources that refused the fetch tool, the terms that are unclear, and the subject ids.

studies.title: Diercks, Katz and Wright, 'Kalshi and the Rise of Macro Markets', FEDS 2026-010

measures.cause: At the merge of PR 115 the adopted cover was 16. The change of the class ids made it 24: 13 new classes are NWS products that the two adopted NWS sources already read. The layers came after: the 24 classes have 2 adopted sources on 2 paths with no shared part, but one origin, the NWS. A parent class counts its sources at each leaf code, so no class has 2 origins at this time. This rule also made market.crypto a gap, because its two planned sources give different children. No adapter is new, so no new signal reaches a person.

measures.cause: Round 2 adopts the USGS feed for geo.earthquake. The class now has 2 adopted sources on 2 paths with no shared part, and 2 origins: the USGS and the US alerting authorities of the NWS API. So the adopted cover is 25 and the origin cover is 1. The second origin is weak: the NWS API carries only the rare earthquake alerts of the authorities, not each event. The layers do not measure the share of the events that each source carries. The earthquake alerts of the authorities can come from ShakeAlert, a system of the USGS. Then the class has one origin. A later round examines it.

notes: The public paths of the ODIN Web API are /odi, /odi/{utilityId}, /odi/map, /odi/status and /odi/data/{dataId}. The paths under /odin need a token of OAuth 2.0 client credentials.
The path /odi gives the active outages. With view=county it gives one total for each county. It has the filters stateCd and countyCd, and pages of up to 1000 records.
At 2026-11-16 06:45 UTC the status list had 159 utilities: 158 with a report of the past 24 hours, 136 with one of the past hour, and 9 with an error. The county path gave 86 counties.
The county dataset of ODIN on the Open Energy Data Portal had 220 records and states no license. Its last change was 7 hours before the read, so it is not the live path.

The outage maps of KUBRA Storm Center read JSON files from the servers of KUBRA. KUBRA publishes no API documentation, and its terms cover only its payment services. The terms of the two utilities forbid automated reading without written consent. So the round plans no outage map.
The match of the EMSC events to the USGS events used a time of 20 seconds and a distance of 100 km. The largest time difference of a match was 6.3 seconds.
The USGS feed had 41 events in the time of the EMSC answer. EMSC had 30 of them. Each of the 11 misses was a small event of a US network.
Of the 24 events in the areas of the US networks, 13 were in EMSC, each with the solution of a US network. Of the 17 events outside them, EMSC had 17, and NEIC was the author of 9.
So in the United States, EMSC is a second path to the solutions of the US networks, not a second origin. Outside it, EMSC gives the solutions of many agencies and of NEIC.
